original_questions.prompt: A 63-year-old with a 40 pack-year smoking history has a CT pulmonary angiogram for pleuritic pain, negative for embolus. It shows a single solid nodule in the right lower lobe with a mean diameter of 4 mm, smooth margins and no calcification. There is no known malignancy and no immunosuppression. What does the 2017 Fleischner guidance recommend?
choices: An optional single CT at 12 months
A CT at 6 months and at 18 months
A CT at 3 months, then PET-CT
Immediate biopsy of the nodule
original_questions.answer: An optional single CT at 12 months
original_questions.explain: For a single solid nodule under 6 mm, low-risk patients need no routine follow-up, and high-risk patients are offered an optional CT at 12 months. The word optional carries the argument: even in a heavy smoker a nodule this size has under about a one per cent chance of being a cancer, so the recommendation is a discussion rather than an instruction, and features such as an upper lobe location, spiculation, coexisting emphysema or fibrosis, or a family history legitimately tip an individual decision. The 6 to 12 month schedule with a second scan at 18 to 24 months belongs to the 6 to 8 mm band, and going straight to PET-CT or biopsy at 4 mm subjects the patient to tests that cannot answer the question at that size. Note also what the study is: an incidental finding on a scan done for something else, which is the only setting the guidance addresses.

original_questions.prompt: A first CT in a 60-year-old shows a solitary part-solid nodule in the left upper lobe, 14 mm overall with a 4 mm solid component. There are no symptoms of infection and no prior imaging exists. What is the next step?
choices: Repeat thin-section CT at 3-6 months
PET-CT to assess the solid component
CT-guided biopsy of the solid part
Lobectomy for presumed adenocarcinoma
original_questions.explain: The first duty with any subsolid nodule seen once is to establish that it is real and persistent, because a large proportion of subsolid opacities are transient: infection, haemorrhage, focal inflammation and organising pneumonia all look like this and are gone in three months. So a repeat thin-section CT at 3 to 6 months precedes any decision. If it persists with a solid component still under 6 mm, annual CT for five years follows, since a persistent part-solid nodule is often on the adenocarcinoma spectrum but grows slowly and the solid part is the invasive part. PET-CT at a 4 mm solid component is below the useful resolution of the technique and lepidic tumour is poorly avid in any case; percutaneous biopsy of a 4 mm target is unreliable; and resecting before persistence is established treats a proportion of patients for pneumonia they have already recovered from.

original_questions.prompt: A persistent 12 mm pure ground-glass nodule is referred with a request for PET-CT to confirm that it is benign. The nodule shows no FDG uptake above background lung. How should that result be used?
choices: It does not lower the risk from this appearance
It confirms the nodule is benign, so discharge
It shows the nodule is inflammatory, repeat in 3 months
It means the nodule should be resected without delay
original_questions.answer: It does not lower the risk from this appearance
original_questions.explain: FDG uptake tracks glucose metabolism and, in practice, viable cell density. A persistent pure ground-glass nodule is characteristically atypical adenomatous hyperplasia, adenocarcinoma in situ or minimally invasive adenocarcinoma, all of which grow along intact alveolar walls with very little cellular bulk, so a negative scan is expected whether the lesion is benign or malignant, and it carries almost no information. Acting on it ends a surveillance programme that the guidance asks to run to five years, and the thing being watched for over those years is the appearance or growth of a solid component. PET-CT earns its place with solid nodules above roughly 8 mm, and even there it has the mirror-image problem of false positives from granulomatous and other inflammatory disease. Small size and low cell density are its two blind spots, and this nodule has both.

original_questions.prompt: A CT report flags a new 5 mm nodule. On review it is a smooth, homogeneous, lentiform solid nodule in the right lower zone, in contact with the oblique fissure with its long axis lying along the fissure, and it has a thin linear tail running to the pleura. It was present at the same size on a scan four years earlier. What follow-up is needed?
choices: No follow-up: this is a lymph node
A CT at 12 months for stability
A CT at 3 months, then 12 months
PET-CT to characterise it further
original_questions.answer: No follow-up: this is a lymph node
original_questions.explain: A typical perifissural nodule is an intrapulmonary lymph node: solid, smooth, homogeneous, oval or triangular, in contact with or within a few millimetres of a fissure or the pleura, usually below the level of the carina, and often with a septal tail running to the pleural surface. In screening cohorts these have proved essentially never to be malignant, and the guidance exempts them from follow-up on morphology alone. Four years of stability settles the matter independently, since two years of unchanged size is the conventional evidence of benignity for a solid nodule. That convention is worth keeping separate in your mind from subsolid disease, where it does not hold: adenocarcinoma in situ can sit unchanged for years, so two years of stability in a ground-glass nodule proves nothing.

original_questions.prompt: A 9 mm solid nodule found incidentally contains a focus measuring -70 HU on a region of interest placed on a thin section, together with a coarse central clump of calcification. What follows?
choices: Fat and calcium here indicate a hamartoma
The low attenuation indicates a cavity
This appearance requires PET-CT staging
This warrants CT again in 3 to 6 months
original_questions.answer: Fat and calcium here indicate a hamartoma
original_questions.explain: Macroscopic fat inside a pulmonary nodule, conventionally in the region of -40 to -120 HU, is close to diagnostic of a hamartoma, and with coarse popcorn-like calcification the diagnosis is secure and the nodule needs no follow-up at all. The rare exceptions worth knowing are lipoid pneumonia and fat-containing metastases from liposarcoma or renal cell carcinoma, which do not resemble this. Two cautions govern the measurement. It must be made on thin sections, because partial volume averaging with adjacent air can fabricate a fat-like value in a small nodule. And the calcification pattern must be one of the benign ones, which are central, laminated, diffusely solid and popcorn: eccentric or stippled calcium does not exclude malignancy, since a carcinoma can engulf a pre-existing granuloma. Recognising the nodule that needs nothing is as much a part of the algorithm as recognising the one that needs everything.

original_questions.prompt: A 31-year-old two years after renal transplantation, on tacrolimus and mycophenolate, has three new solid nodules of 4 to 5 mm on a CT performed for fever. A trainee proposes an optional CT at 12 months, quoting the Fleischner recommendations. What is wrong with that?
choices: The guideline excludes patients like this one
The nodules are multiple, so the interval halves
The nodules are too small to be measured reliably
The patient's age puts her in the low-risk column
original_questions.answer: The guideline excludes patients like this one
original_questions.explain: The 2017 recommendations apply to incidental nodules in immunocompetent patients aged 35 and over who have no known primary malignancy, and they explicitly do not apply within a lung cancer screening programme, where a structured reporting system takes over. This patient fails on two counts, and each on its own would be enough. Immunosuppressed, new nodules with fever are an infection question until proved otherwise, and invasive fungal disease, nocardia, mycobacteria and post-transplant lymphoproliferative disorder are answered in days by a repeat scan, bronchoscopy or empirical treatment, not in a year. Under 35, the prior probability of lung cancer is low and the accumulated radiation of surveillance is comparatively costly, so benign and infective causes are managed clinically. Knowing when an algorithm does not apply is the part of it that most often gets skipped.

original_questions.prompt: A part-solid nodule under annual surveillance measures 15 mm overall on this year's scan and on last year's, but its solid component has gone from 4 mm to 9 mm over those 12 months. The patient has no new symptoms. What should happen?
choices: Refer for PET-CT, biopsy or resection
Continue annual CT to complete five years
Repeat CT at 3 months to confirm growth
Treat for infection and rescan in 6 weeks
original_questions.answer: Refer for PET-CT, biopsy or resection
original_questions.explain: In a part-solid nodule the solid component is the invasive component, and it drives both the risk and, if this becomes a cancer diagnosis, the T category. A growing solid component, or one reaching 8 mm, takes the nodule out of surveillance and into PET-CT, sampling or resection. The trap the case is built around is that the overall diameter never changed: had only the total size been recorded, the nodule would have been called stable and left for another year, which is why the solid component is measured separately on every study, on the same thin-section lung-window images. Waiting a further three months to confirm growth repeats a measurement already made over a whole year and delays treatment of a lesion that has declared itself. At 9 mm the solid component is also large enough for PET-CT to be informative, which it was not when the component was 4 mm.

original_questions.prompt: On a 1 mm axial section an incidental solid nodule measures 7.0 mm along its long axis and 3.8 mm along the perpendicular short axis on the same image. Applying the Fleischner measurement convention, what size in millimetres is recorded for this nodule? Answer with the number alone.
original_questions.explain: The convention is the average of the long-axis and short-axis diameters obtained on the same image, rounded to the nearest whole millimetre, measured on thin sections in a lung window. Here 7.0 and 3.8 average to 5.4, which is recorded as 5 mm, and that places an elongated nodule whose longest measurement is 7 mm below the 6 mm threshold, so a low-risk patient needs no routine follow-up. Reporting the long axis alone would have committed the same patient to a year of surveillance for the same lesion. The convention exists because it is reproducible rather than because it is the truth about the object: a nodule is not a sphere, and averaging two orthogonal diameters is simply a rule two readers can both follow. Semi-automated volumetry is more reproducible again, and the guidance gives the equivalents, roughly 100 cubic millimetres at 6 mm and 250 at 8 mm, for departments that measure volume instead.

original_questions.prompt: A solid nodule has a mean diameter of 6.0 mm. Treating it as a sphere, what mean diameter in millimetres corresponds to exactly one doubling of its volume? Give it to one decimal place. Answer with the number alone.
original_questions.explain: Volume scales with the cube of diameter, so a doubling needs a diameter multiplied by the cube root of two, that is 1.26: 6.0 becomes 7.56, or 7.6 mm to one decimal place. The lesson is in how small that step is. A whole doubling of tumour volume shows up as 1.6 mm on a ruler, which is inside the interobserver variability of manual measurement of a small nodule, so a solid nodule can double without any reader being able to prove it, and two readers can disagree about growth that never happened. That is the argument for volumetry, which measures the quantity that is actually doubling, and for long enough intervals that real growth outruns the noise. Volume doubling times of roughly 100 to 400 days characterise most solid lung cancers; much faster than that suggests infection or inflammation, and much slower suggests a benign lesion or an indolent subsolid tumour, whose doubling times commonly run to several years.

original_questions.prompt: A solitary pure ground-glass nodule of 9 mm is still present and unchanged on the confirmatory CT performed at 9 months. Counting from the first scan, for how many years in total does the 2017 Fleischner guidance recommend that surveillance continue? Answer with the number alone.
original_questions.explain: A solitary ground-glass nodule of 6 mm or more gets a CT at 6 to 12 months to confirm that it persists, then CT every two years out to five years in total. Persistence has ruled out infection and haemorrhage; it has emphatically not ruled out tumour, because the lesions that produce a persistent ground-glass nodule grow so slowly that the two-year stability rule used for solid nodules carries no weight here. Five years is not a claim that risk falls to zero afterwards, but a judgement about the yield of continued scanning against its radiation and cost. What the surveillance is watching for is a change in character rather than a change in size: the appearance of a solid component, or the growth of one, is the event that signals invasion and moves the patient from watching to treatment.

original_questions.prompt: The 2017 revision moved the threshold below which no routine follow-up is advised from 4 mm up to 6 mm. Justify that change, and say what it implies for a 5 mm solid nodule in a heavy smoker.
original_questions.answer: The evidence, largely from screening cohorts, is that a solid nodule under 6 mm carries a risk of malignancy below about one per cent even in high-risk people, and that a year of CT surveillance changes very little for such a nodule, because growth of that magnitude sits inside the measurement noise and because a cancer that small is usually still curable when it later declares itself. Set against that near-zero yield are real costs: the radiation of repeated scans, the financial cost, the anxiety of being under surveillance, and the cascade of further imaging and procedures that follows a followed nodule. Raising the threshold therefore removes surveillance from a very large number of people with little loss of cancer detection. For a 5 mm nodule in a heavy smoker the guidance offers an optional CT at 12 months rather than requiring one: the judgement is handed to the clinician and the patient, and an upper lobe location, spiculation, emphysema or fibrosis, or a family history are legitimate reasons for an individual to take it.
original_questions.explain: A threshold in a guideline is a statement about the balance of harms rather than a claim about biology, and reading it that way explains both the change and the hedging around it. Below 6 mm the yield of surveillance is so low that the harms of scanning dominate, so the recommendation is withdrawn; the nodules did not become safer in 2017. It also explains why the high-risk column says optional rather than recommended: at that risk level the decision is genuinely close, and the guideline declines to make it for the patient. The corollary for reporting is to give the referrer what the decision needs, which is the mean diameter measured by the convention, the solid or subsolid character, the location, the margin, and an explicit statement of which follow-up row the nodule falls in, rather than a bare description of a nodule.

original_questions.prompt: A nodule reported as 7 mm last year is reported as 9 mm today, and the patient is referred as growing. Before accepting growth, list the conditions that must match between the two measurements, and say which single technique removes most of the remaining disagreement.
original_questions.answer: Both measurements should come from thin sections, ideally 1 mm and at most about 1.5 mm, displayed in a lung window with comparable settings, made by the same convention, which is the average of long and short axis on the same image, and read in the same plane; a nodule measured on a 5 mm series last year against a 1 mm series today will appear to change for purely technical reasons, and partial volume averaging in the thicker series usually understates it. Respiratory phase and patient positioning should be comparable, since a nodule in dependent lung can be measured differently in atelectatic surroundings. Above all, the prior images should be re-measured personally rather than the previous report's number being taken on trust, since the two numbers being compared were produced by different readers. Manual diameter carries an interobserver variability of a millimetre or two, which is the same size as the change being argued about, and semi-automated volumetry is substantially more reproducible: it measures the quantity that actually doubles, and expresses change as a volume doubling time.
original_questions.explain: Most reported growth in small nodules is measurement, not biology, and the discipline that prevents the error is comparing like with like and doing the comparison yourself. Two habits carry most of the benefit. First, always open the prior study rather than reading its report, because the number in a report is a different reader's judgement on possibly different data. Second, state the technique the measurement came from in your own report, so that whoever compares next year knows what to match. The deeper point is about what growth means once established: a change in diameter is hard to interpret, whereas a volume doubling time places the lesion on a scale where roughly 100 to 400 days is typical of solid malignancy, faster suggests inflammation, and much slower suggests something indolent or benign.

original_questions.prompt: An incidental solid nodule is found on a CT performed for another reason. Put these five decisions in the order that gets the follow-up right, beginning with the one that can stop the algorithm before any measurement is made.
original_questions.explain: First, whether the guidance applies to this patient at all: under 35, immunosuppressed, a known primary malignancy, or a nodule found within a screening programme, and it does not, so any table you consult afterwards gives the wrong answer confidently. Second, whether the nodule is already diagnosed by its morphology, since fat with popcorn calcification makes a hamartoma, a benign calcification pattern makes a granuloma, and a typical perifissural nodule makes an intrapulmonary lymph node, and each of these ends the matter with no follow-up at all. Third, solid or subsolid, because the two run on different tables and different timescales. Fourth, the mean diameter by the averaging convention, which selects the row. And last, the patient's risk category, which chooses between columns and, in the smallest band, between an optional scan and none. Risk comes last because it modifies a recommendation rather than generating one, and applying it first is how a heavy smoker with an obvious hamartoma ends up in five years of surveillance.

It confirms the nodule is benign, so discharge
It shows the nodule is inflammatory, repeat in 3 months
It means the nodule should be resected without delay

owner_proposed_questions.explain: The complete homogeneous, smooth, lentiform or triangular perifissural pattern is characteristic of an intrapulmonary lymph node and ordinarily requires no nodule follow-up in the qualifying incidental context. owner_proposed_questions.prompt: An incidental 9 mm solid nodule in an immunocompetent adult without known primary cancer contains macroscopic fat confirmed with a small intranodular ROI on thin, nonsharpened CT sections, with coarse popcorn-like calcification. The fat ROI excludes adjacent air and edge pixels. What follows?
choices: The imaging pattern strongly supports a benign hamartoma
The low attenuation indicates a cavity
This appearance requires PET-CT staging
This warrants CT again in 3 to 6 months
owner_proposed_questions.answer: The imaging pattern strongly supports a benign hamartoma
owner_proposed_questions.explain: Verified intranodular macroscopic fat and a characteristic benign calcification pattern strongly support a benign hamartoma pattern, usually removing the need for nodule surveillance in this clinical context. The imaging diagnosis is not new histological confirmation.

owner_proposed_questions.prompt: An incidental part-solid nodule in an immunocompetent adult without known primary cancer is assessed on comparable thin-section CT examinations 12 months apart. owner_proposed_questions.prompt: A nodule reported as 7 mm last year is reported as 9 mm today. Before accepting growth, describe the measurements and technical factors that should be compared. Name a technique that can improve reproducibility, and state what must remain consistent for that technique.

Compare thin sections, the same mean-diameter convention and plane of greatest dimension, comparable lung window settings, reconstruction thickness and kernel, respiratory state and relevant contrast or surrounding-lung differences. Record any limitation instead of assuming the scans are interchangeable. Semi-automated volumetry can improve reproducibility, but comparisons require the same validated method and consistent software version and segmentation performance. A volume doubling time requires actual measurements and an elapsed time; neither diameter growth nor a growth rate alone establishes histology.

independent_amended_questions.prompt: An immunocompetent 60-year-old without known primary cancer has an incidental solitary part-solid nodule,14 mm overall with a 4 mm solid component. There are no symptoms of infection and no prior imaging. Applying Fleischner 2017, what is the next step?
choices: Repeat thin-section CT at 3-6 months
PET-CT to assess the solid component
CT-guided biopsy of the solid part
Lobectomy for presumed adenocarcinoma
independent_amended_questions.explain: For this qualifying solitary part-solid nodule of at least 6 mm overall, repeat thin-section CT at 3–6 months to assess persistence. If it persists without growth and the solid component remains below 6 mm, annual CT through 5 years is recommended. This is not the initial schedule for every subsolid nodule: a qualifying solitary pure ground-glass nodule at least 6 mm uses 6–12 months initially. Transient inflammatory opacities remain a differential, and persistence does not itself establish a cancer diagnosis.

independent_amended_questions.prompt: A persistent 12 mm pure ground-glass nodule is referred with a request for PET-CT to confirm that it is benign. The nodule shows no FDG uptake above background lung. How should that result be used?
choices: It does not establish benignity or justify ending CT surveillance
It confirms the nodule is benign, so discharge
It shows the nodule is inflammatory, repeat in 3 months
It means the nodule should be resected without delay
independent_amended_questions.answer: It does not establish benignity or justify ending CT surveillance
independent_amended_questions.explain: A negative FDG PET result does not reliably exclude malignancy in a persistent pure ground-glass nodule. Low uptake and limited spatial resolution reduce PET sensitivity for this morphology. CT morphology, risk, eligibility and interval change determine further assessment; PET negativity alone should not end indicated CT surveillance. Ground-glass attenuation is not a histological diagnosis, and infection or other benign processes can share the appearance. PET may help selected larger solid nodules, while inflammatory disease can also produce positive uptake.

independent_amended_questions.prompt: A CT report flags a new 5 mm nodule. On review it is a smooth, homogeneous, lentiform solid nodule in the right lower zone, in contact with the oblique fissure with its long axis lying along the fissure, and it has a thin linear tail running to the pleura. It was present at the same size on a scan four years earlier. What follow-up is needed?
choices: No nodule follow-up for this typical benign perifissural morphology
A CT at 12 months for stability
A CT at 3 months, then 12 months
PET-CT to characterise it further
independent_amended_questions.answer: No nodule follow-up for this typical benign perifissural morphology
independent_amended_questions.explain: The complete homogeneous, smooth, lentiform or triangular perifissural pattern is characteristic of an intrapulmonary lymph node and ordinarily requires no nodule follow-up in the qualifying incidental context. Fissural proximity alone is insufficient, and a suspicious or atypical lesion must not be dismissed on location alone. The report should describe the observed pattern rather than assert histology from CT. This case also supplies genuine four-year comparison imaging; the LIDC source case does not.

independent_amended_questions.prompt: An incidental 9 mm solid nodule in an immunocompetent adult without known primary cancer contains macroscopic fat confirmed with a small intranodular ROI on thin, nonsharpened CT sections, with coarse popcorn-like calcification. The fat ROI excludes adjacent air and edge pixels. What follows?
choices: The imaging pattern strongly supports a benign hamartoma
The low attenuation indicates a cavity
This appearance requires PET-CT staging
This warrants CT again in 3 to 6 months
independent_amended_questions.answer: The imaging pattern strongly supports a benign hamartoma
independent_amended_questions.explain: Verified intranodular macroscopic fat and a characteristic benign calcification pattern strongly support a benign hamartoma pattern, usually removing the need for nodule surveillance in this clinical context. A single negative point value near adjacent air is insufficient because partial volume can simulate fat. Use thin nonsharpened sections and a small ROI; record technique and uncertainty. Diffuse, central, laminated and popcorn patterns are considered benign, whereas eccentric or stippled calcium alone does not exclude malignancy. The imaging diagnosis is not new histological confirmation.

independent_amended_questions.prompt: A 31-year-old two years after renal transplantation, on tacrolimus and mycophenolate, has three new solid nodules of 4 to 5 mm on a CT performed for fever. A trainee proposes an optional CT at 12 months, quoting the Fleischner recommendations. What is wrong with that?
choices: The guideline excludes patients like this one
The nodules are multiple, so the interval halves
The nodules are too small to be measured reliably
The patient's age puts her in the low-risk column
independent_amended_questions.answer: The guideline excludes patients like this one
independent_amended_questions.explain: Fleischner 2017 does not apply to patients under 35, immunocompromised patients, patients with known primary cancer, or screening examinations. This patient is both young and immunocompromised. New nodules with fever warrant prompt assessment in the actual clinical context, including infectious and other causes; the incidental small-nodule follow-up table supplies neither a treatment plan nor a safe delay. Investigation and treatment depend on clinical findings, severity, immune status and relevant specialist assessment.

independent_amended_questions.prompt: An incidental part-solid nodule in an immunocompetent adult without known primary cancer is assessed on comparable thin-section CT examinations 12 months apart. It remains 15 mm overall, but remeasurement confirms the solid component has grown from 4 mm to 9 mm. What should happen?
choices: Refer for PET-CT, biopsy or resection
Continue annual CT to complete five years
Repeat CT at 3 months to confirm growth
Treat for infection and rescan in 6 weeks
independent_amended_questions.answer: Refer for PET-CT, biopsy or resection
independent_amended_questions.explain: Confirmed enlargement of the solid component is suspicious despite unchanged total diameter and warrants further clinical evaluation, with PET-CT, sampling or resection considered according to the individual case. A CT dense component correlates with invasive burden in relevant adenocarcinomas but does not prove histological invasion. Record both total size and the solid component on comparable thin-section images. A persistent solid component of at least 6 mm is already highly suspicious; the management discussion becomes more concerning with growth or a component exceeding 8 mm. Negative PET would not reliably exclude a low-uptake malignancy.

independent_amended_questions.prompt: On a 1 mm CT image in the plane showing the nodule’s largest dimensions, an incidental solid nodule measures 7.0 mm along its long axis and 3.8 mm along the perpendicular short axis on that same image. Applying the Fleischner measurement convention, what size in millimetres is recorded? Answer with the number alone.
independent_amended_questions.explain: The convention is the average of the long-axis and short-axis diameters obtained on the same image, rounded to the nearest whole millimetre, measured on thin sections in a lung window. Here 7.0 and 3.8 average to 5.4, which is recorded as 5 mm, and that places an elongated nodule whose longest measurement is 7 mm below the 6 mm threshold, so a low-risk patient needs no routine follow-up. Reporting the long axis alone would have committed the same patient to a year of surveillance for the same lesion. The convention exists because it is reproducible rather than because it is the truth about the object: a nodule is not a sphere, and averaging two orthogonal diameters is simply a rule two readers can both follow. Semi-automated volumetry is more reproducible again, and the guidance gives the equivalents, roughly 100 cubic millimetres at 6 mm and 250 at 8 mm, for departments that measure volume instead.

independent_amended_questions.prompt: A solid nodule has a mean diameter of 6.0 mm. Treating it as a sphere, what mean diameter in millimetres corresponds to exactly one doubling of its volume? Give it to one decimal place. Answer with the number alone.
independent_amended_questions.explain: For the declared sphere, volume is proportional to diameter cubed: 6.0 × 2^(1/3) = 7.5595 mm, recorded here as 7.6 mm. That 26 percent diameter increase can be difficult to distinguish from measurement variation in a small nodule; detectability depends on the method and comparable source images. Validated volumetry can improve reproducibility but also requires consistent technique and software. Actual volume doubling time needs two measured volumes and their elapsed interval. Growth rates overlap between benign and malignant nodules; slow growth or apparent stability alone does not exclude malignancy. This calculation neither proves tumour growth in the reference case nor determines histology.

independent_amended_questions.prompt: A solitary pure ground-glass nodule of 9 mm is still present and unchanged on the confirmatory CT performed at 9 months. Counting from the first scan, for how many years in total does the 2017 Fleischner guidance recommend that surveillance continue? Answer with the number alone.
independent_amended_questions.explain: For a qualifying solitary pure ground-glass nodule at least 6 mm, the initial 6–12 month CT evaluates persistence, followed by CT every 2 years until 5 years from the initial examination. The answer is 5 years in total. Persistence is not proof of a neoplasm or proof that all infectious causes have been excluded. New or increasing solidity, growth, suspicious morphology and the clinical context can change the plan; the surveillance interval is not a guarantee of benignity.

independent_amended_questions.prompt: The 2017 revision moved the threshold below which no routine follow-up is advised from 4 mm up to 6 mm. Justify that change, and say what it implies for a 5 mm solid nodule in a heavy smoker.
independent_amended_questions.answer: The threshold reflects the usually low malignancy risk of solid nodules under 6 mm and the balance between surveillance benefit and radiation, anxiety, financial cost and downstream procedures. The risk is often below 1 percent even in high-risk screening cohorts, but suspicious morphology or upper-lobe location can increase it. For a 5 mm incidental solid nodule in a qualifying heavy smoker, Fleischner 2017 permits an optional CT at 12 months, with patient risk, morphology, comorbidity and preferences guiding the decision. The threshold does not prove the nodule benign or guarantee later curability.
independent_amended_questions.explain: No routine follow-up and optional follow-up are recommendations for defined clinical categories, not biological guarantees. Preserve the low-risk/high-risk distinction, the solid/subsolid distinction and single/multiple context. Suspicious morphology can justify a different individualized choice even for a small lesion.

independent_amended_questions.prompt: A nodule reported as 7 mm last year is reported as 9 mm today. Before accepting growth, describe the measurements and technical factors that should be compared. Name a technique that can improve reproducibility, and state what must remain consistent for that technique.
independent_amended_questions.answer: Reopen and remeasure the prior images rather than compare report numbers alone. Compare thin sections, the same mean-diameter convention and plane of greatest dimension, comparable lung window settings, reconstruction thickness and kernel, respiratory state and relevant contrast or surrounding-lung differences. Record any limitation instead of assuming the scans are interchangeable. Semi-automated volumetry can improve reproducibility, but comparisons require the same validated method and consistent software version and segmentation performance. A volume doubling time requires actual measurements and an elapsed time; neither diameter growth nor a growth rate alone establishes histology.
independent_amended_questions.explain: Diameter and volume measurements both contain uncertainty. The current case supplies no evidence that most reported growth is artefactual. A change around 2 mm should be interpreted with acquisition quality, measurement reproducibility and the actual prior examination. Volumetry does not remove all disagreement, and a volume doubling time is not a stand-alone benign-versus-malignant test.

independent_amended_questions.prompt: An incidental solid nodule is found on a CT performed for another reason. Put these five decisions in the order that gets the follow-up right, beginning with the one that can stop the algorithm before any measurement is made.
independent_amended_questions.explain: This is a teaching sequence for the stated incidental-nodule task. First establish whether the chosen guideline applies. Then assess the complete benign imaging pattern; verified fat, characteristic calcium or typical perifissural morphology can support a benign imaging interpretation without supplying histological confirmation. Distinguish solid from subsolid, use the appropriate measurement convention, and combine those observations with clinical risk, the actual single/multiple context, prior images and patient preferences. Risk informs real decisions throughout; this ordered exercise is not a universal algorithm or a substitute for the relevant guideline branch.

bounded_explain_only_amendments.before: Volume scales with the cube of diameter, so a doubling needs a diameter multiplied by the cube root of two, that is 1.26: 6.0 becomes 7.56, or 7.6 mm to one decimal place. The lesson is in how small that step is. A whole doubling of tumour volume shows up as 1.6 mm on a ruler, which is inside the interobserver variability of manual measurement of a small nodule, so a solid nodule can double without any reader being able to prove it, and two readers can disagree about growth that never happened. That is the argument for volumetry, which measures the quantity that is actually doubling, and for long enough intervals that real growth outruns the noise. Volume doubling times of roughly 100 to 400 days characterise most solid lung cancers; much faster than that suggests infection or inflammation, and much slower suggests a benign lesion or an indolent subsolid tumour, whose doubling times commonly run to several years.
bounded_explain_only_amendments.after: For the declared sphere, volume is proportional to diameter cubed: 6.0 × 2^(1/3) = 7.5595 mm, recorded here as 7.6 mm. That 26 percent diameter increase can be difficult to distinguish from measurement variation in a small nodule; detectability depends on the method and comparable source images. Validated volumetry can improve reproducibility but also requires consistent technique and software. Actual volume doubling time needs two measured volumes and their elapsed interval. Growth rates overlap between benign and malignant nodules; slow growth or apparent stability alone does not exclude malignancy. This calculation neither proves tumour growth in the reference case nor determines histology.

bounded_explain_only_amendments.before: First, whether the guidance applies to this patient at all: under 35, immunosuppressed, a known primary malignancy, or a nodule found within a screening programme, and it does not, so any table you consult afterwards gives the wrong answer confidently. Second, whether the nodule is already diagnosed by its morphology, since fat with popcorn calcification makes a hamartoma, a benign calcification pattern makes a granuloma, and a typical perifissural nodule makes an intrapulmonary lymph node, and each of these ends the matter with no follow-up at all. Third, solid or subsolid, because the two run on different tables and different timescales. Fourth, the mean diameter by the averaging convention, which selects the row. And last, the patient's risk category, which chooses between columns and, in the smallest band, between an optional scan and none. Risk comes last because it modifies a recommendation rather than generating one, and applying it first is how a heavy smoker with an obvious hamartoma ends up in five years of surveillance.

Then assess the complete benign imaging pattern; verified fat, characteristic calcium or typical perifissural morphology can support a benign imaging interpretation without supplying histological confirmation. Distinguish solid from subsolid, use the appropriate measurement convention, and combine those observations with clinical risk, the actual single/multiple context, prior images and patient preferences. Risk informs real decisions throughout; this ordered exercise is not a universal algorithm or a substitute for the relevant guideline branch.

protocol_amendment.before: Use the complete acquired thorax with contiguous thin sections at most 1.5 mm, typically 1 mm, and explicit coverage/quality limitations. Record acquired thickness separately from reconstruction interval and pixel spacing.
protocol_amendment.after: Use the complete acquired thorax with contiguous thin reconstructed sections at most 1.5 mm, typically 1 mm, and explicit coverage/quality limitations. Record nominal reconstructed section thickness separately from reconstruction centre spacing and pixel spacing. Record acquisition collimation only when independently documented; do not infer it from DICOM SliceThickness.

primary_evidence.supports: 26percent/100–400day population statement is supported, not the subject of a factual-error finding. Individual decisions need morphology/risk/context; no source histology is supplied.
Measurement uncertainty depends on study/method; no growth-rate or stability threshold definitely excludes malignancy.
Nominal reconstructed slice thickness and centre spacing are distinct; neither alone proves acquisition collimation.
Separate screening pathway; do not blend Lung-RADS and Fleischner thresholds.

The79groups are a conditional floor. Generic requirements need explicit actual case/structure/timepoint instantiation and thoracic expert review before claiming every reported structure is represented.
